stem: A major source used to reconstruct the social history of this period (kinship, caste, family) is the great Sanskrit epic, the:
solution: A major source used in this chapter to reconstruct the social history of early India (family, kinship, marriage, caste, and class) is the great Sanskrit epic, the 'Mahabharata'. The Mahabharata — one of the two great Sanskrit epics (the other being the Ramayana) — is a vast text, centred on a great war between two groups of cousins (the Kauravas and the Pandavas), but containing a huge amount of material on society, ethics, philosophy, and statecraft. Historians study the Mahabharata (critically) as a window into the social values, kinship, and other aspects of the society of the period in which it was composed (over several centuries). Understanding that the Mahabharata is a key source for this chapter is a prelims point. A major source for reconstructing the social history of this period is the Sanskrit epic, the Mahabharata.

stem: The Mahabharata is centred on a conflict/war between two groups of cousins, the Kauravas and the:
solution: The Mahabharata is centred on a great conflict (and ultimately a devastating war, fought at Kurukshetra) between two groups of cousins belonging to the same ruling family (the Kuru clan): the Kauravas (the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra, led by Duryodhana) and the Pandavas (the five sons of Pandu — Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, and Sahadeva). The struggle between these cousins over the kingdom/throne forms the central story of the epic. This story of a conflict within a kinship group is itself used by historians to explore ideas about kinship, family, and succession. Understanding that the Mahabharata is about the Kauravas vs the Pandavas is a prelims point. The Mahabharata is centred on a war between two groups of cousins — the Kauravas and the Pandavas.

stem: In the society described, the ideal form of family/succession was based on __________ descent (tracing descent through the father's line).
solution: In the society described in the sources (like the Mahabharata), the ideal/valued form of family and succession was based on patriliny (patrilineal descent) — tracing descent through the male/father's line (from father to son). Under patriliny, sons could claim their father's resources (including the throne, in the case of kings) when he died, and the succession normally passed from father to son. This patrilineal ideal is why, for example, the epic's central conflict is over which set of sons (cousins) should inherit the kingdom, and why the birth of sons was so desired. (There were some exceptions and variations, but patriliny was the norm/ideal being upheld.) Understanding that patriliny (descent through the father) was the ideal is a prelims point. The ideal form of family/succession was based on patrilineal descent (tracing descent through the father's line).

stem: The society was divided (in the ideal Brahmanical scheme) into four __________ (social orders/classes): Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras.
solution: In the ideal Brahmanical scheme (set out in texts like the Dharmashastras), society was divided into four 'varnas' (social orders/classes): (1) the Brahmanas (priests, teachers, scholars); (2) the Kshatriyas (rulers, warriors, and administrators); (3) the Vaishyas (farmers, traders, and merchants); and (4) the Shudras (who were meant to serve the other three varnas — labourers, artisans, servants). This four-fold varna order (the 'chaturvarna' system) was the theoretical framework of caste/class in Brahmanical thought — a hierarchical ordering of society. Understanding the four varnas is a key prelims point. Society was divided (ideally) into four varnas: Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras.

stem: According to the Brahmanical scheme, the varna at the top of the social hierarchy was the:
solution: According to the Brahmanical scheme (as laid down in the Dharmashastras, composed by Brahmanas), the varna placed at the top of the social hierarchy was the Brahmanas (the priests, teachers, and scholars). The Brahmanas claimed the highest status and various privileges. Below them were the Kshatriyas (rulers/warriors), then the Vaishyas (farmers/traders), and at the bottom the Shudras (servants/labourers). (Later, groups considered outside/below even the Shudras — 'untouchables' — were placed at the very bottom.) It is important to note that this hierarchy was the ideal/claim of the Brahmanical texts (which the Brahmanas themselves composed), and the actual social reality was often more complex and did not always match it. Understanding that the Brahmanas were placed at the top is a prelims point. In the Brahmanical scheme, the Brahmanas (priests) were placed at the top of the social hierarchy.

stem: The texts that laid down the norms/rules for society (including the varna order, duties, and conduct), composed by Brahmanas, are the:
solution: The Dharmashastras (and the earlier Dharmasutras) are the Sanskrit texts, composed by Brahmanas (from around the 5th century BCE onwards, the most famous being the Manusmriti), that laid down the norms, rules, and codes of conduct for society. They prescribed: the varna order and the duties/occupations proper to each varna; rules about marriage, family, inheritance, and gender; the duties (dharma) of people in different social positions and stages of life; laws and punishments; and so on. These texts represent the Brahmanical ideal of how society ought to be organised (they are prescriptive/normative). Historians use them (critically) to understand Brahmanical social ideals — while recognising that actual practice often differed. Understanding the Dharmashastras (Brahmanical normative texts) is a prelims point. The Dharmashastras (and Dharmasutras) are the Brahmanical texts that laid down the norms/rules for society, including the varna order.

stem: The most famous of the Dharmashastra texts, a code laying down rules for society and conduct, is the:
solution: The most famous of the Dharmashastra texts is the 'Manusmriti' (the Laws of Manu / Manava Dharmashastra), compiled around the 2nd century BCE – 2nd century CE. It is a code that lays down detailed rules for society and personal conduct — covering the varna order and the duties of each varna, the rules for the different stages of life, marriage and family, the position and duties of women, law and justice, and much else. The Manusmriti is a very important (and much-discussed) text for understanding the Brahmanical social order and its ideals (and its rigid, hierarchical, and patriarchal norms). Understanding the Manusmriti (the most famous Dharmashastra) is a prelims point. The most famous Dharmashastra text is the Manusmriti (the Laws of Manu).

stem: The Brahmanical texts prescribed 'endogamy' — the rule that people should marry:
solution: The Brahmanical texts prescribed 'endogamy' — the rule/practice of marrying within one's own group or caste (specifically, within a defined kin group or jati). Under endogamy, a person was expected to marry someone from the same social group (the same varna/jati), and marriage outside the group was disapproved of. Endogamy was (and is) an important feature of the caste system — it kept the castes separate and hereditary (since caste was passed down within groups that married among themselves), maintaining the boundaries between castes. (This contrasts with 'exogamy' — marrying outside a particular group, like one's own gotra/clan.) Understanding endogamy (marrying within the group) is a prelims point. Endogamy is the rule that people should marry within their own group/caste (a feature of the caste system).

stem: A patrilineal succession (father to son) was important especially for __________, who wished to pass on their kingdom/throne to their sons.
solution: Patrilineal succession (the passing of position/property from father to son) was especially important for kings/rulers, who wished to pass on their kingdom, throne, and power to their (male) heirs — their sons. This is why the birth of sons (male heirs) was so important and desired in ruling families, and why the central conflict of the Mahabharata is precisely a dispute among cousins (sons of two brothers) over who should inherit the kingdom. So the concern with patrilineal succession is especially prominent in the context of kings and ruling families. Understanding that patrilineal succession mattered most for kings/rulers is a prelims point. Patrilineal succession (father to son) was especially important for kings/rulers, who wished to pass their kingdom to their sons.

stem: In this patriarchal society, according to the Brahmanical norms, women were generally expected to be __________ and were placed under the control of male relatives (father, husband, son).
solution: In this patriarchal society, according to the Brahmanical norms (e.g., the Manusmriti), women were generally expected to be subordinate to men, and were placed under the control/guardianship of their male relatives at different stages of life — a woman was to be under the control of her father in childhood, her husband in her married life, and her son in old age (she was not to be independent). Women's roles were largely confined to the domestic sphere (marriage, motherhood, and running the household). This reflects the patriarchal character of the society and the subordinate position it assigned to women (in the Brahmanical ideal — though actual women's lives and roles were more varied). Understanding the subordinate position prescribed for women is a prelims point. In this patriarchal society, women were expected to be subordinate to men, under the control of their father, husband, or son.

stem: The 'gotra' was a system among the Brahmanas (and later others) by which people were classified into __________ (clans, traced from a common ancestor/rishi).
solution: The 'gotra' was a classification (especially among the Brahmanas, and later adopted more widely) by which people were grouped into clans/lineages, each gotra being traced (nominally) from a common ancestor — typically one of the ancient rishis (sages). Two rules were associated with the gotra: (1) women were expected to give up their father's gotra and adopt their husband's gotra on marriage; and (2) members of the same gotra could not marry each other (gotra exogamy — one had to marry outside one's own gotra). The gotra system is used by historians (e.g., studying the gotras of the wives of the Satavahana rulers) to explore kinship, marriage rules, and social norms. Understanding the gotra (clan classification) is a prelims point. The gotra was a system classifying people into clans/lineages, traced from a common ancestor (rishi).

stem: One rule associated with the gotra was that members of the same gotra were NOT allowed to __________ each other.
solution: One important rule associated with the gotra was that members of the same gotra were NOT allowed to marry each other — that is, one had to marry someone from a different gotra (this is 'gotra exogamy'). Since a gotra was regarded as a group descended from a common ancestor (rishi), its members were considered kin, and marriage within the gotra was prohibited (as it would be like marrying a relative). (The other rule was that a woman adopted her husband's gotra on marriage, giving up her father's.) So same-gotra marriage was forbidden. Understanding this gotra rule (no same-gotra marriage) is a prelims point. Members of the same gotra were not allowed to marry each other (gotra exogamy).

stem: Groups that were placed OUTSIDE/BELOW the four varnas, and were treated as 'untouchable' and made to do the most menial/degrading work, were called (among other terms):
solution: Groups that were placed outside and below the four varnas — regarded as the lowest of the low, and subjected to 'untouchability' (they were considered 'polluting', so their touch or even presence was to be avoided by the 'higher' castes) — were made to do the most menial, degrading, and 'impure' tasks (such as handling corpses, cleaning, and dealing with refuse). One such group named in the texts was the 'Chandalas' (who were, for example, assigned the task of handling and disposing of dead bodies, and were subjected to many degrading restrictions). The existence of such 'untouchable' groups (outcastes) at the very bottom, suffering severe discrimination, is one of the harshest and most unjust features of the caste/varna system. Understanding this (untouchables like the Chandalas, outside the varnas) is a prelims point. Groups outside/below the four varnas, treated as 'untouchable' and made to do menial work, included the Chandalas.

stem: The 'jati' (in contrast to the four broad varnas) refers to:
options: the many smaller castes/sub-castes (often based on occupation) into which society was actually divided
solution: The 'jati' refers to the many smaller castes/sub-castes into which society was actually divided — a much larger and more numerous set of groups than the four broad varnas. While the varna scheme divided society into just four ideal categories, in reality people belonged to numerous jatis, which were often based on occupation (e.g., a jati of potters, weavers, ironsmiths, etc.), and which had their own rules (of marriage — endogamy, of food, of conduct) and their own place in the local social order. The Brahmanical texts tried to fit these jatis into the four-varna framework, but the jatis were the actual, on-the-ground units of caste. So jati = the actual castes/sub-castes (as opposed to the four theoretical varnas). Understanding the jati (vs varna) distinction is a prelims point. The jati refers to the many smaller castes/sub-castes (often occupation-based) into which society was actually divided (vs the four broad varnas).

stem: The Brahmanical claim that the varna order was divinely ordained/fixed was NOT always accepted; in reality, social mobility and change DID occur — for example, some __________ became kings despite not being Kshatriyas by birth.
options: people of non-Kshatriya origin (like the Mauryas or others)
solution: The Brahmanical claim that the varna order was divinely ordained and fixed (unchangeable, with each person's status determined by birth) was NOT always accepted or true in practice — in reality, social mobility and change DID occur. For example, several ruling dynasties came from origins that were not 'Kshatriya' by the strict Brahmanical definition: the Mauryas (whose origins are described as non-Kshatriya/low in some traditions), the Shungas, and others rose to become kings; and various groups (including foreign rulers like the Shakas and Kushanas, and local chieftains) attained kingly/high status regardless of their birth-varna. Also, occupations were not always strictly hereditary. So the neat, fixed varna hierarchy was an ideal that did not fully match the more fluid social reality. Understanding that social mobility occurred (contrary to the fixed-varna ideal) is a prelims point. The fixed-varna ideal was not always the reality — social mobility occurred, e.g., people of non-Kshatriya origin became kings.

stem: The Mahabharata was composed and added to over a long period. Historians therefore treat it as a source that:
options: gives exact facts for a single year
reflects the ideas and society of the several centuries over which it was composed (and must be used critically)
solution: The Mahabharata was not composed at one time by one author, but was composed, expanded, and added to over a very long period (roughly from about 500 BCE to 400 CE — nearly a thousand years, with layers added by many hands). Because of this, historians treat it as a source that reflects the ideas, values, and social conditions of the several centuries over which it was composed (rather than of a single moment), and they must use it critically — distinguishing its layers, allowing for its being partly a literary/didactic work (with a message, not pure history), and being careful about what it can and cannot tell us. So the Mahabharata is a rich but complex source, to be used critically and with awareness of its long, layered composition. Understanding how historians treat the Mahabharata (as a layered source, used critically) is a prelims-relevant point. The Mahabharata was composed over a long period, so historians treat it as reflecting the ideas of several centuries, to be used critically.

stem: The critical edition of the Mahabharata (a major scholarly project to prepare a reliable text) was prepared under the leadership of __________ (at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute).
solution: The critical edition of the Mahabharata — a major, decades-long scholarly project to prepare a reliable, standard text of the epic by comparing the many surviving manuscripts — was prepared under the leadership of the Sanskrit scholar V.S. Sukthankar (beginning in 1919, at the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute in Pune). Scholars collected and compared hundreds of manuscripts of the Mahabharata from across the country (in different scripts), and worked to establish the text and note the variations. This monumental project (which took several decades) is an example of the careful scholarly work involved in using such a source, and it is mentioned in the chapter. Understanding the critical edition (Sukthankar) is a prelims-relevant point. The critical edition of the Mahabharata was prepared under the leadership of V.S. Sukthankar.

stem: The Brahmanical ideal that a woman's most important duty was to be a devoted wife and mother reflects the __________ nature of the society.
solution: The Brahmanical ideal that a woman's most important duties/roles were to be a devoted, obedient wife and a mother (bearing children, especially sons, and serving her husband and family) reflects the patriarchal nature of the society — a social system in which men held the dominant power and authority (in the family and society), and women were subordinate and largely confined to domestic roles centred on marriage and motherhood. Under this patriarchy, women's identity and worth were defined largely in relation to men (as daughters, wives, and mothers), and they were denied independence and many rights. So this ideal for women is an expression of the society's patriarchy. Understanding this (the ideal for women reflecting patriarchy) is a prelims point. The ideal that a woman's chief duty was to be a devoted wife and mother reflects the patriarchal nature of the society.

stem: Assertion (A): Historians do not accept the Brahmanical texts' description of society as a simple, accurate picture of reality. Reason (R): These texts were composed by Brahmanas to present an IDEAL (prescriptive) order, and the actual social practice often differed from and did not fully follow these norms. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that historians do not accept the Brahmanical texts' description of society (e.g., the neat four-varna hierarchy) as a simple, accurate picture of the actual reality. And the reason is (R) that these texts (the Dharmashastras, like the Manusmriti) were composed by Brahmanas to present an IDEAL, prescriptive order — how they thought society OUGHT to be organised (with the Brahmanas on top) — rather than an objective description of how it actually was; and the actual social practice often differed from these norms (there was social mobility, the norms were not always followed, and the reality was more fluid and complex). Because the texts give a biased, idealised prescription (not a factual description), historians must treat them critically and not take them as literal reality — so R correctly explains A. Understanding this (Brahmanical texts = prescriptive ideal, not actual reality) is a key prelims-relevant point. Historians don't take the Brahmanical texts as accurate reality, because they present an ideal (prescriptive) order, and actual practice often differed from those norms.

stem: In the Mahabharata, Draupadi is described as being married to all five __________ brothers — an example of polyandry.
solution: In the Mahabharata, Draupadi is described as being married to all five Pandava brothers (Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula, and Sahadeva) — one wife shared by five brothers. This is an example of polyandry (a woman having more than one husband, here specifically 'fraternal polyandry' — brothers sharing a wife). This unusual practice is discussed by historians because it appears to go against the more common Brahmanical norm (which favoured polygyny — a man having several wives — rather than polyandry); the epic itself offers various explanations for it. It is used to explore the variety and complexity of marriage practices/norms in early India. Understanding Draupadi's polyandrous marriage is a prelims-relevant point. In the Mahabharata, Draupadi was married to all five Pandava brothers — an example of polyandry.

stem: The practice of a man having more than one wife is called __________ (which was permitted, especially for elite men, in this society).
solution: Polygyny is the practice of a man having more than one wife (at the same time). This was permitted and practised in early Indian society, especially among elite/wealthy and ruling-class men (kings often had several wives, for various reasons — alliances, producing heirs, status). (This is different from 'polyandry' — a woman having several husbands, which was rare, e.g., Draupadi; and from 'monogamy' — one husband and one wife.) The Brahmanical norms generally accepted polygyny for men. So a man having multiple wives = polygyny. Understanding polygyny is a prelims-relevant point. Polygyny is the practice of a man having more than one wife, which was permitted, especially for elite men.

stem: The 'Manusmriti' generally allowed __________ to inherit the paternal property (in the patrilineal system).
solution: In the patrilineal system upheld by the Manusmriti (and the Dharmashastras generally), it was the sons who generally inherited the paternal property (the father's estate was divided among the sons after his death). Daughters were generally NOT given a share of the paternal landed property/estate in the same way (their access to the family property was very limited — though a woman could have some wealth of her own, called 'stridhana'). This inheritance rule (property passing to sons) both reflected and reinforced the patrilineal and patriarchal nature of the society (and the subordinate economic position of women). Understanding that sons (not daughters) inherited the paternal property is a prelims-relevant point. The Manusmriti generally allowed sons (not daughters) to inherit the paternal property.

stem: The wealth that a woman could receive at the time of her marriage (as gifts), which was considered her own property, was called:
solution: 'Stridhana' (literally 'woman's wealth') was the wealth/property that a woman could receive at the time of her marriage — in the form of gifts (given to her by her parents/relatives, and others). This stridhana was considered her own property, which she could keep and, in principle, pass on to her children (her sons could inherit it, and it was not to be taken by her husband against her will). Stridhana was one of the few forms of property that a woman could own in this largely patriarchal society (where women generally did not inherit the main paternal landed estate). So stridhana was a woman's own marriage-gift wealth. Understanding stridhana is a prelims-relevant point. Stridhana was the wealth (marriage gifts) that a woman could receive and keep as her own property.

stem: The story of __________, a forest-dwelling boy (a Nishada) who was refused instruction in archery by Drona (because of his low birth) and was later made to give up his thumb, illustrates caste discrimination in the Mahabharata.
solution: The story of Ekalavya in the Mahabharata illustrates the discrimination based on birth/caste. Ekalavya was a forest-dwelling boy — a Nishada (a member of a forest/hunting tribe, considered 'low-born'). He wished to learn archery from the great teacher Drona, but Drona refused to teach him (because he was low-born, and because Drona had promised that his royal pupil Arjuna would be the best archer). Ekalavya nonetheless practised on his own (before a clay image of Drona) and became a superb archer — even surpassing Arjuna. Drona then demanded, as his 'teacher's fee' (dakshina), Ekalavya's right thumb — which Ekalavya gave, crippling his archery (so that Arjuna would remain the best). This story is used to show how the society discriminated against low-born/tribal people and denied them opportunities. Understanding the Ekalavya story (as an example of caste/birth discrimination) is a prelims-relevant point. The story of Ekalavya (a Nishada refused instruction by Drona, and made to give up his thumb) illustrates caste/birth discrimination in the Mahabharata.

stem: The epic character __________, though a great warrior, faced humiliation/discrimination because he was thought to be of low (Suta/charioteer) origin rather than a Kshatriya.
solution: Karna, in the Mahabharata, though one of the greatest warriors of the epic, faced repeated humiliation and discrimination because he was believed/known to be of low origin — he had been raised by a charioteer (Suta) family, so he was regarded as a 'Suta' (charioteer, a group of lower status), not a Kshatriya (warrior-noble) by birth. Because of his supposed low birth, Karna was, for example, taunted and refused the right to compete or be treated as an equal by the Kshatriya princes on some occasions. (In fact, the epic reveals he was actually of royal/Kshatriya birth — the son of Kunti — but he did not know this for most of his life.) The story of Karna is used to explore the importance and injustice of birth-based status. Understanding Karna's story (discrimination for supposed low birth) is a prelims-relevant point. Karna, though a great warrior, faced discrimination because he was thought to be of low (Suta/charioteer) origin, not a Kshatriya.

stem: The Mahabharata (traditionally attributed to the sage __________) is regarded as an 'itihasa' (history/'thus it was').
solution: The Mahabharata is traditionally attributed to the sage Vyasa (Veda Vyasa) as its author/compiler (Valmiki, by contrast, is the traditional author of the other great epic, the Ramayana). The Mahabharata is regarded in the Indian tradition as an 'itihasa' — a word often translated as 'history' (literally 'thus it was' / 'so indeed it was'), meaning a narrative of things believed to have really happened (as opposed to pure fiction). So the tradition treats the Mahabharata as itihasa, composed by Vyasa. (Historians, of course, treat it as a layered literary source to be used critically.) Understanding that Vyasa is the traditional author and the epic is called 'itihasa' is a prelims-relevant point. The Mahabharata, traditionally attributed to the sage Vyasa, is regarded as an 'itihasa' (history).

stem: The Mahabharata is a very long epic; because of its enormous length (about 100,000 verses), it is also called the __________ ('collection of a hundred thousand [verses]').
solution: The Mahabharata is an enormously long epic — in its final form it contains about 100,000 verses (shlokas), making it one of the longest poems/epics in the world. Because of this length, it is also called the 'Shatasahasri Samhita' — meaning the 'collection (samhita) of a hundred thousand (shatasahasri) [verses]'. It grew to this vast size through additions and expansions over the long period of its composition (from a possibly shorter original core). So the Mahabharata is known as the Shatasahasri Samhita for its 100,000 verses. Understanding this (the ~100,000-verse Shatasahasri Samhita) is a prelims-relevant point. The Mahabharata, with about 100,000 verses, is also called the 'Shatasahasri Samhita' ('collection of a hundred thousand').

stem: The famous philosophical/religious text the 'Bhagavad Gita' (Krishna's teachings to Arjuna) is a part of the:
solution: The 'Bhagavad Gita' (the 'Song of the Lord') — the famous philosophical/religious dialogue in which the god Krishna gives spiritual/moral teachings to the warrior Arjuna (on the eve of the Kurukshetra battle, when Arjuna is filled with doubt about fighting his kinsmen) — is a part of the Mahabharata (it forms a section of the epic's Bhishma Parva). Though it is part of the epic, the Bhagavad Gita is also revered as an independent sacred text (one of the most important texts of Hindu philosophy and devotion). So the Gita is embedded within the Mahabharata. Understanding that the Bhagavad Gita is part of the Mahabharata is a prelims point. The Bhagavad Gita (Krishna's teachings to Arjuna) is a part of the Mahabharata.

stem: The Dharmashastras laid down eight forms of marriage; of these, the FIRST four were considered 'good'/approved, and the most valued was the __________ form (the gift of the daughter to a suitable man).
solution: The Dharmashastras laid down eight forms/types of marriage. The first four of these were considered the 'good'/approved forms, and among them the most valued/ideal was the 'Brahma' form of marriage — in which the father gave away his daughter (kanyadana, the 'gift of a maiden'), suitably adorned, to a man of good character and learning (of the same varna), without receiving any payment/bride-price. This form (the honourable gift of the daughter to a worthy groom) was regarded as the highest and most respectable. (The other, disapproved forms included marriage by purchase — 'Asura', by mutual love — 'Gandharva', by capture — 'Rakshasa', etc.) Understanding the Brahma form (the most valued marriage) is a prelims-relevant point. Of the eight forms of marriage, the most valued was the 'Brahma' form — the gift of the daughter to a suitable man.

stem: The Satavahana ruler Gautamiputra Satakarni's mother, Gautami Balashri, issued an inscription. This is used to study __________ and the practice of naming after the mother's line among the Satavahanas.
solution: The Satavahana rulers (of the Deccan) are interesting for the study of kinship because, although their succession was patrilineal (father to son), they used 'metronymics' — names derived from the mother's name. For example, 'Gautamiputra' Satakarni means 'Satakarni, son of Gautami' (Gautami being his mother's name/gotra). His mother, Gautami Balashri, issued a famous inscription praising her son. Historians study this (the metronymics, and the roles of women like Gautami Balashri) to explore kinship, the position of women, and gotra/naming practices among the Satavahanas — showing an interesting mix (patrilineal succession but names after the mother). Understanding this (Satavahana metronymics/kinship, and Gautami Balashri's inscription) is a prelims-relevant point. The Satavahanas used names derived from the mother's line (metronymics), studied via inscriptions like that of Gautami Balashri (mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni).

stem: Groups like the Nishadas (forest-dwellers/hunters), who lived outside the settled varna society, are an example of __________ that the Brahmanical order tried to place at a low status.
solution: Groups like the Nishadas (forest-dwellers and hunters, such as the tribe to which Ekalavya belonged) are examples of tribal/forest peoples who lived, at least partly, outside the settled agrarian varna society and its norms. The Brahmanical order tended to view such tribal/forest peoples as low/outside the fourfold varna scheme (as 'others'), and it tried to place them at a low status (or as outside/below the varnas). The relationship between the settled varna society and these forest/tribal peoples (and how the latter were viewed, incorporated, or discriminated against) is one of the themes explored — showing that the Brahmanical order faced (and tried to fit in) groups that did not conform to its neat scheme. Understanding this (tribal/forest peoples like the Nishadas, placed at low status) is a prelims-relevant point. The Nishadas (forest-dwellers/hunters) are an example of tribal peoples living outside settled varna society, whom the Brahmanical order placed at a low status.

stem: The Chinese Buddhist pilgrim __________ (who visited India around the 5th century CE) recorded observations about the harsh treatment of the 'untouchables' (Chandalas).
solution: Fa Xian (Faxian), a Chinese Buddhist pilgrim who travelled in India around 400 CE (the early 5th century, during the Gupta period), recorded observations about Indian society in his travel account — including notes on the harsh treatment and segregation of the 'untouchables' (such as the Chandalas). For example, he noted that the Chandalas were made to live apart, and had to strike a piece of wood to warn others of their approach (so that people could avoid contact with them). His account is valuable outside evidence of the practice of untouchability and social discrimination. (Later Chinese pilgrims like Xuanzang/Hsuan Tsang also visited.) Understanding Fa Xian's observations (on untouchables) is a prelims-relevant point. The Chinese pilgrim Fa Xian (Faxian) recorded the harsh treatment of the 'untouchables' (Chandalas) in India.

stem: The Brahmanical texts prescribed occupations for each varna: the Vaishyas were assigned occupations like agriculture, __________, and trade.
solution: The Brahmanical texts assigned specific occupations/duties to each varna. The Vaishyas were assigned the occupations of agriculture (farming), cattle-rearing/pastoralism, and trade/commerce (and money-lending) — that is, the productive economic activities of farming, herding, and business. (For comparison: the Brahmanas were assigned study, teaching, and performing rituals; the Kshatriyas were assigned warfare, protection, and administration/ruling; and the Shudras were assigned the single 'occupation' of serving the other three varnas.) So the Vaishyas' prescribed occupations were farming, herding, and trade. Understanding the occupations assigned to the Vaishyas is a prelims-relevant point. The Vaishyas were assigned occupations like agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade.

stem: The Brahmanical texts assigned the Shudras only ONE occupation, namely:
solution: According to the Brahmanical texts (the Dharmashastras), the Shudras (the fourth and lowest of the four varnas) were assigned only one occupation/duty: to serve the other three varnas (the Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas). That is, the Shudras were meant to be servants/labourers who served and worked for the 'higher' three varnas — they were denied the occupations and privileges assigned to the others (they were not to study the Vedas, perform rituals, rule, or engage in independent trade in the ideal scheme). This shows the subordinate, service position assigned to the Shudras at the bottom of the fourfold order. Understanding the occupation assigned to the Shudras (serving the others) is a prelims-relevant point. The Brahmanical texts assigned the Shudras only one occupation: serving the other three varnas.

stem: The Brahmanas tried to fit new social groups (like conquering foreigners, or new occupational groups) into the varna framework, showing that the caste system was, in practice, __________ (not entirely fixed).
options: somewhat flexible/adaptable (able to absorb new groups)
solution: The Brahmanas tried to fit new social groups — such as conquering foreign rulers (like the Shakas, Kushanas, and other 'outsiders' who became kings), new occupational/craft groups (jatis), and forest/tribal peoples being brought into the settled society — into the varna framework (for example, by giving them a place in the hierarchy, or by treating some as 'fallen Kshatriyas', or by creating rules for 'mixed' castes). This effort to accommodate/absorb new groups shows that the caste system was, in practice, somewhat flexible and adaptable (not entirely fixed/rigid) — it could and did change over time and absorb new groups (even as it maintained its hierarchical and birth-based principles). So the reality was more dynamic than the 'fixed, unchanging' ideal. Understanding this (the caste system's practical flexibility in absorbing new groups) is a prelims-relevant point. The Brahmanas fit new groups into the varna framework, showing the caste system was, in practice, somewhat flexible/adaptable (not entirely fixed).

stem: The game of __________ (in which Yudhishthira gambled away his kingdom, his brothers, himself, and Draupadi) is a famous episode of the Mahabharata.
solution: The game of dice (a gambling match) is a famous and pivotal episode of the Mahabharata. In it, the eldest Pandava, Yudhishthira, was drawn into a rigged game of dice (against the Kauravas, with Shakuni playing/cheating on Duryodhana's behalf), and he lost everything — staking and losing his wealth and kingdom, then his brothers, then himself, and finally their common wife Draupadi. Draupadi was then dragged into the assembly and humiliated. This episode (and the injustice done to Draupadi and the Pandavas) is a turning point that leads toward the great war, and it is much discussed — for its drama and for what it reveals about the values, kinship, and gender norms of the society. Understanding the dice-game episode is a prelims-relevant point. The game of dice, in which Yudhishthira gambled away his kingdom, brothers, self, and Draupadi, is a famous episode of the Mahabharata.

stem: Some religious/philosophical movements of this period (like Buddhism) __________ the Brahmanical claim of birth-based caste superiority.
solution: Some religious and philosophical movements of this period — notably Buddhism (and also Jainism, and later various devotional/bhakti and reformist movements) — questioned and challenged the Brahmanical claim of birth-based caste superiority (the idea that a person's status/worth was fixed by the varna they were born into). The Buddha, for example, taught that a person's worth depended on their conduct/actions (their moral qualities), not on their birth-caste, and Buddhism was, in principle, open to people of all varnas. This critique of the birth-based caste hierarchy by movements like Buddhism shows that the Brahmanical order was not accepted by everyone — it was contested. Understanding that Buddhism challenged birth-based caste is a prelims-relevant point. Movements like Buddhism questioned/challenged the Brahmanical claim of birth-based caste superiority.

stem: Historians distinguish between 'prescriptive' texts (which say how society OUGHT to be) and 'descriptive' evidence (of how it actually WAS). The Dharmashastras are mainly:
solution: The Dharmashastras (like the Manusmriti) are mainly prescriptive (normative) texts — they prescribe how society OUGHT to be organised and how people OUGHT to behave (laying down the ideal rules, duties, and norms, from the Brahmanical point of view) — rather than describing how society actually WAS in practice. This distinction is very important for historians: because the Dharmashastras are prescriptive, we cannot simply assume that the society actually followed all their rules (the ideal and the reality often differed). To find out how society actually was, historians must look for other, more 'descriptive' evidence (like inscriptions, accounts of practices, and archaeological findings) and use the prescriptive texts critically. Understanding that the Dharmashastras are prescriptive (not descriptive) is a key prelims-relevant point. The Dharmashastras are mainly prescriptive (normative) texts — saying how society ought to be — not descriptions of how it actually was.

stem: The Mahabharata (and the Ramayana) were later translated into many regional languages and retold in different versions, showing that these epics:
options: remained living, evolving traditions, retold and adapted over the centuries across the subcontinent
solution: The Mahabharata (and the Ramayana) were, over the centuries, translated into many regional/vernacular languages and retold in numerous different versions and adaptations (with variations in the stories, added local elements, and different emphases) across the different regions and communities of the subcontinent (and beyond, in Southeast Asia). This shows that these epics were NOT static, one-time texts, but remained living, evolving traditions — continually retold, reinterpreted, adapted, and made meaningful for different times, places, and audiences. This ongoing, evolving life of the epics is itself of interest to historians (and shows how the epics have been part of the culture for a very long time). Understanding this (the epics as living, evolving, retold traditions) is a prelims-relevant point. The Mahabharata and Ramayana were translated and retold in many versions over the centuries, showing they remained living, evolving traditions.

stem: The 'exogamy' rule (marrying OUTSIDE a particular group, like one's own gotra) is the OPPOSITE of:
solution: 'Exogamy' — the rule/practice of marrying OUTSIDE a particular defined group (for example, outside one's own gotra/clan, as required by the gotra rule) — is the opposite of 'endogamy', which is the rule of marrying WITHIN one's group (for example, within one's own caste/jati). In fact, the two often operated together in the caste system: a person was expected to marry within their broad caste (endogamy) but outside their immediate clan/gotra (exogamy). So exogamy (marry-outside) and endogamy (marry-within) are the two opposite marriage rules. Understanding the exogamy/endogamy contrast is a prelims-relevant point. 'Exogamy' (marrying outside a group, like one's gotra) is the opposite of 'endogamy' (marrying within one's group/caste).

stem: The presence of both a patrilineal succession AND the use of the mother's name (metronymics) among the Satavahanas shows that kinship practices were:
options: varied and could combine different elements (not always fitting one neat pattern)
solution: The presence of BOTH a patrilineal succession (the throne passing from father to son) AND the use of metronymics (names derived from the mother's name, like 'Gautamiputra' — son of Gautami) among the Satavahanas shows that kinship practices in early India were varied and could combine different elements — they did not always fit one neat, uniform pattern. Here, an essentially patrilineal system nonetheless honoured the mother's line in naming — a mixture of features. This is a good example of how the actual kinship practices were more complex and diverse than any single simple rule, reminding historians not to assume uniformity. Understanding this (kinship practices were varied/mixed) is a prelims-relevant point. The Satavahanas' patrilineal succession combined with metronymics shows that kinship practices were varied and could combine different elements.

stem: The word 'kula' in the context of kinship refers to:
solution: In the context of kinship, the Sanskrit word 'kula' refers to the family or household — the kin group/lineage (the people related by blood/kinship who form a family unit or lineage). (Related kinship terms include 'jnati' — kinfolk/relatives in general, and 'vamsha' — lineage/dynasty/family line.) These terms were used in the texts to speak of families, lineages, and kin groups. So 'kula' = family/household (kin group). Understanding the term 'kula' is a prelims-relevant point. In kinship, 'kula' refers to the family/household (the kin group).

stem: The stories of the Mahabharata (like those of Ekalavya, Karna, and Draupadi) are used by historians to explore the __________ of the society (its values, kinship, caste, and gender attitudes).
solution: Historians use the stories and characters of the Mahabharata (like those of Ekalavya, Karna, Draupadi, Yudhishthira, and others) not just as tales, but as windows into the social norms and attitudes of the society in which the epic was composed — exploring its values, its ideas about kinship and family, its caste/varna attitudes and the discrimination based on birth (as in the Ekalavya and Karna stories), its gender norms and the position of women (as in the Draupadi episodes), and its ideals of duty (dharma), honour, and conduct. So these stories are read (critically) for what they reveal about the society's social norms and attitudes. Understanding that historians use the epic's stories to explore social norms is a prelims-relevant point. Historians use the Mahabharata's stories to explore the society's social norms and attitudes (its values, kinship, caste, and gender attitudes).

stem: The four varnas' status was, according to the Brahmanas, determined by __________ (which fixed a person's varna).
solution: According to the Brahmanas (the Brahmanical/Dharmashastra view), a person's varna (and hence their status, duties, and place in the hierarchy) was determined by birth — i.e., a person was born into a particular varna (that of their parents), and this fixed their varna-status for life (it was hereditary and, ideally, unchangeable). This birth-based principle is the essence of the varna/caste system as the Brahmanas presented it — status was ascribed by birth, not achieved by wealth, ability, effort, or choice. (This birth-based idea is precisely what movements like Buddhism criticised, and what the actual social mobility of the period partly contradicted.) Understanding that varna was (in the Brahmanical view) determined by birth is a key prelims-relevant point. According to the Brahmanas, a person's varna/status was determined by birth (it was hereditary and fixed).

stem: Which of the following is an example that shows the ACTUAL social reality sometimes DIFFERED from the ideal varna order?
options: Everyone always followed their varna occupation
Rulers of non-Kshatriya origin (like the Mauryas, or foreign Shaka/Kushana kings) became kings
The Brahmanas were always at the top with no exceptions
Untouchability was always accepted by all
solution: An example that shows the actual social reality sometimes differed from the ideal varna order is that rulers of non-Kshatriya origin — such as the Mauryas (whose origins were described as non-Kshatriya/low in some traditions), and foreign rulers like the Shakas and Kushanas ('outsiders'/mlechchhas) — nevertheless became kings, even though the ideal scheme reserved kingship/ruling for the Kshatriya varna (by birth). This social mobility (people rising to kingship regardless of their birth-varna), along with occupations not always being strictly hereditary and the norms not always being followed, shows that the real society was more fluid and did not perfectly match the rigid, birth-based ideal. So non-Kshatriyas becoming kings is a clear example of the ideal-vs-reality gap. Understanding such examples is a prelims-relevant point. Non-Kshatriyas (like the Mauryas or foreign Shaka/Kushana kings) becoming kings shows that the actual social reality sometimes differed from the ideal varna order.

stem: The subordination of women in this society was reflected in restrictions such as women generally NOT being allowed to __________.
options: study the Vedas / own the main paternal property / have independence (they were controlled by male relatives)
solution: The subordination of women in this patriarchal society (in the Brahmanical norms) was reflected in various restrictions and disabilities, such as: women were generally not allowed to study the Vedas (or perform Vedic rituals independently); they generally could not inherit or own the main paternal (landed) property (their access to property was very limited — mainly the 'stridhana'); and they were denied independence — being kept under the control/guardianship of male relatives (father, husband, son) throughout their lives, and largely confined to the domestic sphere. These restrictions reflect the limited rights and subordinate position assigned to women. (They were NOT, of course, forbidden to eat, have children, or speak — the point is the specific legal/social disabilities.) Understanding the restrictions on women is a prelims-relevant point. Women's subordination was reflected in restrictions like not being allowed to study the Vedas, own the main paternal property, or have independence (being controlled by male relatives).

stem: Assertion (A): The Mahabharata is a valuable source for social history, but it cannot be read simply as a straightforward record of actual events. Reason (R): It is a literary epic, composed and expanded over centuries, mixing history with myth, moral teaching, and later additions, and it upholds certain ideals (so it must be interpreted critically). Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the Mahabharata is a valuable source for social history but cannot be read simply as a straightforward, literal record of actual events. And the reason is (R) that it is a literary epic — composed, expanded, and reworked over several centuries (a layered text), mixing whatever historical kernel it may contain with myth, legend, moral/religious teaching (dharma), and many later additions, and it upholds certain ideals and values (rather than being an objective chronicle). Because of all this, we cannot take its narrative as a literal factual account; instead, historians must interpret it critically — distinguishing its layers, allowing for its literary and didactic nature and its biases, and using it (alongside other sources) as evidence of the ideas, values, and social norms of the times, rather than as a plain record of events. So R correctly explains why the Mahabharata must be read critically (A). Understanding this (the Mahabharata as a layered literary source, to be used critically) is a key prelims-relevant point. The Mahabharata is valuable but not a literal record, because it is a layered literary epic mixing history with myth and moral teaching, so it must be interpreted critically.

stem: Historians reconstruct the social history of c. 600 BCE–600 CE by supplementing the Brahmanical Sanskrit texts with which other important body of evidence?
options: Only oral folk songs collected in modern times
Inscriptions (epigraphic records) and other material sources like coins and sculpture
European travellers' accounts of the 18th century
solution: Historians do not rely on the Brahmanical Sanskrit texts alone; they supplement and cross-check them with other sources — especially inscriptions (epigraphic records, such as the Prakrit inscriptions of the Satavahanas and other dynasties), as well as coins, sculpture, and accounts by visitors like the Chinese pilgrim Fa Xian. This matters because the normative texts give an idealised picture, whereas inscriptions and material evidence can reveal actual social practices (for instance, Satavahana rulers using metronymics, or non-Kshatriyas exercising kingship). Using varied sources critically is essential to reconstruct social realities as opposed to Brahmanical ideals. Inscriptions and material sources are used alongside the Sanskrit texts.

stem: In the Manusmriti, 'stridhana' (a woman's own wealth, such as gifts received at marriage) could be inherited by her children and could NOT be claimed by the husband. This indicates that:
options: Women owned all the land in ancient India
Even within a patriarchal framework, women had some limited, recognised property rights
Property was always held jointly with no individual ownership
Women were forbidden from receiving any gifts
solution: According to the Manusmriti, stridhana (literally 'woman's wealth') — typically gifts received by a woman at the time of her marriage — was regarded as her own; it could be inherited by her children, and the husband had no right to it. This shows that even within an overwhelmingly patriarchal social order that generally subordinated women and placed them under male control, women were nonetheless recognised as having certain limited property rights over specific categories of wealth. At the same time, the text cautioned women against hoarding family property without the husband's permission, reflecting the constraints of the patriarchal system. Stridhana is thus an example of a qualified female entitlement within a broadly male-dominated framework.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Kinship, Caste and Class: Early Societies' is that:
options: Ancient Indian society had no divisions

Early Indian society was structured by kinship (family, patriliny, marriage rules like endogamy and gotra), by the varna/caste system (the ideal four-fold order of Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras — with 'untouchables' below — and the many jatis), and by class and gender (a patriarchal order subordinating women), as reflected in sources like the Mahabharata and the Dharmashastras — but these Brahmanical norms were an IDEAL, and the actual society was more varied, with mobility and change, so the sources must be used critically
solution: The chapter conveys that early Indian society (roughly 600 BCE – 600 CE) was structured and organised along several lines — kinship, caste, and class (and gender) — and it explores these using sources like the great epic the Mahabharata and the Brahmanical normative texts (the Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras, especially the Manusmriti). In terms of kinship and family, it examines the ideal of patriliny (descent and succession through the male/father's line — important especially for kings passing on their kingdoms), and the rules governing marriage (like endogamy — marrying within one's group; and the gotra system — with women adopting the husband's gotra, and marriage forbidden within the same gotra). In terms of caste/class, it examines the Brahmanical ideal of the four-fold varna order (Brahmanas at the top, then Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras) — a hierarchy claimed to be divinely ordained and based on birth — together with the placing of certain groups (the 'untouchables', like the Chandalas) outside and below the varnas, and the reality of the many jatis (actual castes/sub-castes). In terms of gender, it shows the patriarchal character of the society, which subordinated women (placing them under the control of male relatives and confining them largely to domestic roles). Crucially, the chapter stresses that these Brahmanical norms represented an IDEAL/prescriptive order (how the Brahmanas thought society ought to be), and that the actual social reality was often more varied, fluid, and complex — there was social mobility (e.g., people of non-Kshatriya origin becoming kings), the norms were not always followed, and lived experience differed from the ideal — so the sources (the Mahabharata and the Dharmashastras) must be used critically and with awareness of their nature and biases. Understanding how kinship, caste, and class structured early Indian society (in the ideal and in reality), and how to use the sources critically, is the central concern of this chapter. Early Indian society was structured by kinship, the varna/caste order, and gender (a patriarchal system), as set out in the Mahabharata and the Brahmanical texts — but these norms were an ideal, and the actual society was more varied and changing, so the sources must be used critically.
